cards.text: Jesus has just finished telling a parable about a king’s wedding banquet. Then the Pharisees, a group of religious leaders, go out and plot together. The plan? Trap Jesus in His words.

cards.question: The Pharisees don’t show up themselves. They send their own disciples to Jesus, and who else goes with them?

cards.text: They walk up and lay it on THICK: “we know that You are honest and that You teach the way of God in accordance with the truth.” Friend, that’s your boss texting “Quick question” at 4:59 on a Friday.

cards.question: The compliments keep coming. They tell Jesus He pays close attention to external appearance.

cards.text: Compliments done. Here comes the real question, and it’s about money and Caesar, the Roman emperor.

cards.question: They ask Jesus, “So tell us what You think: Is it lawful to pay ___ to Caesar or not?”

cards.text: Big problem for their plan, friend. Jesus knows their evil intent.

cards.question: Jesus sees right through all those compliments. What does He call the people questioning Him?

cards.text: Then Jesus asks for a prop. He says, “Show Me the coin used for the tax.”

cards.question: They bring Jesus a ___, the coin used for the tax.

cards.text: The denarius is right there in front of everybody. “Whose image is this,” He asked, “and whose inscription?”

cards.question: Jesus asks whose image and inscription are on the denarius. What do they answer?
Now Jesus answers their question about the tax. He tells them not to pay it to Caesar.

cards.text: Jesus says, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” They plotted, they recruited, they flattered… and He takes the whole thing apart with one coin.

cards.question: When they hear Jesus’s answer about Caesar and God, they are amazed.

cards.text: So they leave Him and go away with an empty trap. Stick around, friend, because this story’s not done.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 6 quotes "So tell us what You think: Is it lawful to pay ___ to Caesar or not?", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The opening card has four sentences: 'Jesus has just finished telling…', 'Then the Pharisees… plot together.', 'The plan?' and 'Trap Jesus in His words.' That is over the three-sentence limit.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The card states a fact from the previous passage: Jesus has just told a parable about a king's wedding banquet (Matthew 22:1-14). That fact has no reference, and the card cites only Matthew 22:15.

rule.text: Every fact and every verse number comes from that text. Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The Herodians first appear as the answer to card 2. No later card says simply who they are.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The core action on this card is flattery: laying on compliments before springing a trap. A boss texting 'Quick question' at 4:59 on a Friday is a harmless-sounding opener before a hassle, not flattery, so the comparison doesn't share the action.

rule.text: Find the core action in the fact: running away, waiting, being outnumbered, preparing, being surprised. The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Apart from one scene-setting line, the card is just the bare quote. It has almost none of Papa Dorin's voice. The narration also switches from present tense to 'He asked' in past tense.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: 'They recruited' says the Pharisees enlisted the Herodians. Matthew 22:16 only says they sent their disciples along with the Herodians. It leaves open how the two groups are connected.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Card 3 is the only real joke, and card 14 has the only other punchy line. Story cards 7, 9 and 11 read as plain narration. For a story with a flattery-and-trap setup and a one-coin takedown, the walkthrough reads more like a pleasant retelling than laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
